claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090
claims.note: As a report of what the 2024 paper did: title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge', published 14 August 2024; body: isotopic data 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. Pirrie 2026 Conclusions: Clarke et al. (2024) 'proposed that it was derived from the Orcadian Basin of NE Scotland'.

claims.claim: Two years on, scientists still can't agree where it came from.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080; Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090; Parker Pearson 2024 full-text PDF: https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/ (doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13); article page journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.14324/AI.27.1.13
claims.note: Clarke 2026 (online 4 June 2026) still favours NE Scotland: Caithness gives 'the closest match in zircon age structure', 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. Pirrie 2026 (online 5 Nov 2026) questions it: scarce chrome spinel 'may indicate that an origin from this part of NE Scotland needs re-evaluating'; ORS 'from the Scottish Midland Valley to the Anglo-Welsh borderland ... remain possible source areas'; Conclusions 'the provenance of the Altar Stone has yet to be determined with confidence'. Aug 2024 to Nov 2026 is about two years. 'Still' holds in the sense that no source has ever been agreed: Parker Pearson 2024 p.129 'As yet, the actual outcrop from which the Altar Stone was extracted is unknown'. A pedant could note that in 2024 the Clarke and Parker Pearson teams agreed on the Orcadian Basin and the open dispute is a 2026 one; 'still' does not claim a 2024 dispute, so not a fix.

claims.claim: Hook as a viewer who swipes at second two leaves it: 'In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland' (A4)
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Clarke 2026 full text: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080; Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090
claims.note: The first clause is a past-tense report of the 2024 result, true as stated. A viewer who stops there may believe the stone is from Scotland; no cited source shows that false (Clarke 2026 still favours NE Scotland; Pirrie 2026 calls it undetermined and its remaining candidate ORS areas include the Scottish Midland Valley). The '?' over the area and 'SOURCE? / 2026 study questions NE Scotland' plus the title's second sentence carry the dispute early.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090
claims.note: Clarke 2024: U-Pb, Lu-Hf and trace-element data 'for zircon, apatite and rutile from two fragments of the Altar Stone'; heavy-mineral grains 'typically 10-40 µm wide' (tiny); abstract 'remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; apatite components from Caithness and Orkney 'match those from the Altar Stone'. Pirrie 2026 accepts the similarity (and notes the same pattern elsewhere in the Orcadian Basin, still NE Scotland). The script does not claim the match is unique.

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel ...
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'the Altar Stone, a 6 tonne shaped block'; body: 'measuring 4.9 × 1.0 × 0.5 m ... weighing 6 t'. Parker Pearson 2024 p.116: 'a 6-tonne monolith'; Clarke 2026: '6000 kg'.

claims.claim: ... more than seven hundred kilometres? (conditional: 'If so')
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Clarke 2026 full text: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'Such a provenance implies that the Altar Stone ... was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'; body: 'a transport distance of at least 750 km'. 'More than 700' is under that. Clarke 2026's 'some 700 km' is rounder, not contradictory. 'If so' keeps Clarke 2024's own condition ('Such a provenance implies').

claims.claim: The 2024 team suggested it went by sea.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1)
claims.note: Clarke 2024 abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport of such massive cargo from Scotland, navigating topographic barriers, suggests that it was transported by sea.'

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain,
claims.source_checked: Parker Pearson 2024 full-text PDF: https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/ (doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13); article page journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.14324/AI.27.1.13
claims.note: Parker Pearson 2024 p.128: 'Although no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe'; 'The earliest known boats in Britain have been found ... at Ferriby. The earliest of these Early Bronze Age sewn-plank boats (Ferriby 3) dates to 2030-1780 cal bc'. So no Neolithic (New Stone Age) boat is known in Britain at all, which covers either reading of 'late Stone Age'.

claims.claim: ... and another study doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.source_checked: Parker Pearson 2024 full-text PDF: https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/ (doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13); article page journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.14324/AI.27.1.13
claims.note: Parker Pearson 2024 p.128: 'What we know of Early Bronze Age boats ... would suggest that they and their Late Neolithic precursors were unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone in coastal waters.' 'Doubts' = 'unlikely'. 'Another study' is literally true (a different paper), though three of its six authors (Bevins, Ixer, Pearce) are also Clarke 2024 authors; the script does not call it independent.

claims.claim: Overland, on a sledge, that study estimates about eight months of hauling.
claims.source_checked: Parker Pearson 2024 full-text PDF: https://journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/3293/galley/18572/download/ (doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13); article page journals.uclpress.co.uk/ai/article/id/3293/; Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.14324/AI.27.1.13
claims.note: Parker Pearson 2024 p.128: 'a suitably robust wooden sledge ... sliding on wooden rails'; 'such a journey with a large and heavy sledge could take perhaps four times today's time of under two months ... needing eight months or so to haul a stone from northern Scotland to Stonehenge.' 'About' = 'perhaps ... or so'.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: Clarke 2026 full text: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080
claims.note: Clarke 2026 abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement on Salisbury Plain.' Conclusions: 'Glaciation may therefore have provided, at most, partial transport rather than a complete delivery mechanism'; 'Our models do not predict any Late Devensian glacial transport directly to Stonehenge'. Matches 'part of the way, at most' nearly word for word. (The paper also finds even the Dogger Bank stage implausible on timing; leaving that out does not overstate.)

claims.claim: Then, months later, a new study, including three of the 2024 team, looked closer.
claims.source_checked: Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090; Clarke 2024 full text: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07652-1?error=cookies_not_supported (doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1); Clarke 2026 full text: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jqs.70080 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/jqs.70080

Its 13 authors include Bevins, Ixer and Pearce; Clarke 2024's authors are Clarke, Kirkland, Bevins, Pearce, Glorie, Ixer: three shared. 'Looked closer' = abstract 'a detailed multi-proxy characterization of the sedimentology, geochemistry, detrital and diagenetic mineralogy of the Altar Stone'.

claims.source_checked: Pirrie 2026 full text: https://www.lyellcollection.org/doi/full/10.1144/jgs2026-090 (via Firecrawl; doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090); Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090
